title: Degenerative and Demyelinating Diseases of the Nervous System
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers two groups of disease. In neurodegenerative disease, a selected population of neurons dies slowly, usually as a misfolded protein accumulates: Alzheimer, Lewy body, frontotemporal, and supranuclear palsy dementias, ALS, Parkinson, Huntington, and Friedreich ataxia. In demyelinating disease, the immune system strips myelin from axons: multiple sclerosis, ADEM, and transverse myelitis in the central nervous system, and Guillain-Barré syndrome in the peripheral nerves. Vascular dementia, mild cognitive impairment, essential tremor, and cervical dystonia are distinguished from these diseases. Board questions give a pattern of signs and ask for the protein, gene, cell population, or tract responsible. If you know which cells each disease destroys and what those cells normally do, the clinical picture follows.
prerequisites: Upper versus lower motor neuron anatomy and signs (NE-7)
Basal ganglia direct and indirect pathways and dopamine receptors (NE-3, NE-15)
Myelin, oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, and saltatory conduction (NE-2, NE-13)
Ascending and descending spinal cord tracts and their crossing points (NE-3, NE-5)
Trinucleotide repeat expansion and patterns of inheritance (NE-16)

connections.how: Huntington disease and Friedreich ataxia are the model dominant and recessive trinucleotide repeat disorders, and APP and presenilin genes show how gene dosage alters protein processing.
Molecular mimicry and autoreactive T cells explain Guillain-Barré syndrome, ADEM, transverse myelitis, and multiple sclerosis.
Amyloid beta is a beta-pleated sheet protein that stains with Congo red, so Alzheimer plaques and amyloid angiopathy follow the general rules of amyloid deposition.
Vascular dementia is the cumulative result of infarcts, and amyloid angiopathy causes lobar hemorrhage in older adults.
Frataxin deficiency injures cardiomyocytes and pancreatic beta cells, so Friedreich ataxia brings hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes.

terms.def: Progressive loss of a specific population of neurons, usually associated with intracellular or extracellular aggregates of a misfolded protein.
A 38 to 43 amino acid peptide cut from amyloid precursor protein by beta and gamma secretase that aggregates into the core of neuritic plaques.
A microtubule-associated protein that stabilizes axonal microtubules and, when hyperphosphorylated, aggregates into neurofibrillary tangles.
An eosinophilic intracytoplasmic neuronal inclusion composed mainly of alpha-synuclein.
Earlier onset or greater severity of a genetic disease in successive generations, caused by further expansion of an unstable repeat.
Passive enlargement of the ventricles to fill space left by brain atrophy, with normal cerebrospinal fluid pressure.
Loss of the myelin sheath with relative preservation of the axon, which slows or blocks saltatory conduction.
Raised cerebrospinal fluid protein with a normal white cell count, typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Discrete IgG bands on CSF electrophoresis that are absent from serum, showing antibody synthesis within the central nervous system.
Failure of adduction of one eye on lateral gaze, with nystagmus of the abducting eye, caused by a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
A dermatome below which sensation is reduced or lost on both sides, marking a lesion of the spinal cord at or above that segment.
Sustained or intermittent involuntary muscle contraction that produces twisting movements or abnormal postures.

sections.title: Alzheimer disease pathogenesis: amyloid beta, tau, and risk

blocks.text: Alzheimer disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, meaning an acquired decline in memory and other cognitive abilities severe enough to remove independence in daily life. Two abnormal proteins define it: extracellular amyloid beta, which forms plaques, and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau, which forms neurofibrillary tangles.
Processing of amyloid precursor protein

Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is a transmembrane neuronal protein encoded on chromosome 21. Most APP is cut first by alpha secretase, which cleaves inside the amyloid beta sequence and so prevents amyloid beta from forming. When beta secretase (BACE1) cuts first, just outside the membrane, gamma secretase then cuts within the membrane and releases amyloid beta. Presenilin is the catalytic subunit of gamma secretase. Most of the peptide is 40 amino acids long, but the more hydrophobic 42 amino acid form aggregates readily, first into soluble oligomers that impair synapses and then into beta-pleated sheet fibrils that build plaques.

blocks.title: Amyloidogenic processing of APP
steps: APP spans the neuronal plasma membrane
Beta secretase cleaves APP just outside the membrane
Gamma secretase (presenilin) cleaves within the membrane
Amyloid beta 40 and 42 are released
Amyloid beta 42 forms oligomers, then fibrils
Fibrils deposit as plaques and in vessel walls
blocks.caption: Alpha secretase cleavage, the main normal route, cuts inside the amyloid beta sequence and bypasses this pathway.

blocks.text: Tau and neuronal death

Tau binds and stabilizes axonal microtubules, the tracks for axonal transport. In AD, kinases add excess phosphate groups, so tau detaches, self-aggregates into paired helical filaments, and fills the cell body as a neurofibrillary tangle. Microtubules then fall apart, transport of organelles and vesicles fails, and the neuron dies. Amyloid beta is thought to drive tau pathology, but tangle burden and neuron loss correlate with the severity of dementia much better than plaque burden does.

blocks.title: Risk factors for Alzheimer disease
rows: Cumulative protein aggregation and reduced clearance
Strongest risk; most cases after age 65
Less efficient clearance and greater deposition of amyloid beta
Late onset; raises risk in a dose-dependent way but does not determine disease; e2 is protective
Three copies of APP raise amyloid beta production
Plaques and tangles by about age 40; dementia often in the 40s or 50s
Increased total amyloid beta or a higher share of the 42 amino acid form
Altered gamma secretase raises the ratio of amyloid beta 42 to 40
Autosomal dominant, early onset; PSEN1 is the most common familial cause
blocks.caption: Autosomal dominant mutations account for only a small minority of all Alzheimer disease.

blocks.predict: A rare adult with Down syndrome carries a partial trisomy of chromosome 21 that does not include the APP gene. Would you expect early Alzheimer disease?
blocks.explain: No. The early disease in trisomy 21 comes from APP gene dosage, so without an extra APP copy amyloid beta production is not increased.
blocks.check: Compare with the Down syndrome row of the risk factor table and the APP processing flow.

sections.title: Alzheimer disease: gross, microscopic, and clinical findings

blocks.text: Grossly, the AD brain shows diffuse cortical atrophy with narrowed gyri and widened sulci. Atrophy is most severe in the medial temporal lobe (hippocampus and entorhinal cortex) and the association cortex of the temporal, parietal, and frontal lobes, while primary motor, sensory, and visual cortex are relatively spared until late. As brain tissue is lost, the ventricles enlarge passively. This is hydrocephalus ex vacuo: cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure is normal and there is no obstruction. It differs from normal pressure hydrocephalus, in which the ventricles are enlarged out of proportion to the sulci and the triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and dementia appears.

blocks.title: Microscopic lesions of Alzheimer disease
rows: Extracellular amyloid beta core surrounded by dystrophic tau-containing neurites, microglia, and astrocytes
Density is scored in the pathologic diagnosis; amyloid shows apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light
Amyloid beta without surrounding dystrophic neurites
Common in cognitively normal older adults; less specific
Intracellular paired helical filaments of hyperphosphorylated tau, flame-shaped in pyramidal neurons; shown by silver stains
Correlates best with dementia; persists as a ghost tangle after the neuron dies
Amyloid beta in walls of small and medium cortical and leptomeningeal arteries
Weakens vessels; cause of lobar hemorrhage and microbleeds in older adults
Cytoplasmic changes in hippocampal pyramidal neurons
Neuron loss in the nucleus basalis of Meynert
Cholinergic neurons projecting to the cortex
blocks.caption: Definitive diagnosis rests on neuropathology showing plaques and tangles in sufficient density and distribution.

blocks.text: Why memory fails first

Tangles appear first in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus and then spread through the limbic system into the neocortex. The hippocampus is needed to form new declarative memories, so the first symptom is loss of short-term memory for recent events, with repetitive questions and misplaced items, while remote memories are preserved. As the neocortex becomes involved, word-finding difficulty (anomia), visuospatial disorientation such as getting lost, impaired judgment and executive function, and apraxia follow. Late disease brings mutism, incontinence, and immobility, and death often results from aspiration pneumonia or other infection, usually several years to a decade after diagnosis.

Biomarkers reflect the same pathology. CSF amyloid beta 42 is low because the peptide is trapped in plaques rather than circulating, while total and phosphorylated tau are raised as neurons die and release tau. Amyloid PET shows cortical deposits, MRI shows medial temporal atrophy, and FDG-PET shows reduced glucose metabolism in the temporoparietal cortex.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is progressive degeneration of both upper motor neurons (UMNs) in the motor cortex, with their corticospinal and corticobulbar axons, and lower motor neurons (LMNs) in the anterior horn and brainstem motor nuclei. The name describes the pathology: amyotrophic refers to muscle atrophy from denervation, and lateral sclerosis refers to gliosis and hardening of the lateral columns, where the corticospinal tracts run.

About 90% of cases are sporadic and about 10% are familial. Mutations in SOD1, which encodes copper-zinc superoxide dismutase on chromosome 21, act through a toxic gain of function: the mutant protein misfolds and aggregates rather than simply losing enzyme activity. A GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9orf72 is the most common familial cause and also causes frontotemporal dementia, which explains why the two diseases overlap. In nearly all sporadic cases, motor neurons contain cytoplasmic inclusions of the protein TDP-43. Glutamate excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, and impaired axonal transport contribute to cell death.

blocks.title: Upper versus lower motor neuron signs in ALS
rows: Loss of descending inhibition of spinal reflex circuits
Brisk jaw jerk, spastic dysarthria, pseudobulbar affect
blocks.caption: The diagnostic clue in ALS is UMN and LMN signs together in the same region, often in the same limb.

blocks.text: ALS is a pure motor disease. Sensory neurons are not part of the motor system, so sensation is normal. The oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nuclei and Onuf nucleus in the sacral cord (S2 to S4), which supplies the voluntary external urethral and anal sphincters, are relatively resistant, so eye movements and bladder and bowel control are usually preserved until very late. A sensory level, sphincter loss, or abnormal eye movements therefore points to another diagnosis, such as cervical myelopathy from spinal canal narrowing, which can also mix UMN and LMN signs.

Weakness typically begins asymmetrically in a limb or in bulbar muscles and spreads. EMG shows active denervation in several body regions with normal sensory nerve conduction. As phrenic (C3 to C5) and intercostal motor neurons die, ventilation fails, and respiratory failure, often with aspiration, is the usual cause of death, with median survival of about 3 to 5 years from symptom onset.

Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta project to the striatum (caudate and putamen). Dopamine excites the direct pathway through D1 receptors and inhibits the indirect pathway through D2 receptors; both effects lower inhibitory output from the globus pallidus internus to the thalamus, so dopamine facilitates movement.

In Parkinson disease (PD), these pigmented neurons die, so the substantia nigra looks pale on gross section. Surviving neurons contain Lewy bodies, round eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions with a pale halo, composed mainly of aggregated alpha-synuclein. Lewy pathology also affects the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, the olfactory system, and the locus ceruleus, often before the nigra, which explains prodromal loss of smell, constipation, and REM sleep behavior disorder. Motor signs appear only after roughly half of nigral neurons, and most striatal dopamine, are lost. Most PD is sporadic, with misfolded alpha-synuclein, mitochondrial complex I dysfunction, and oxidative stress from dopamine metabolism as central mechanisms; a minority is familial (for example SNCA or LRRK2 mutations, dominant, and PRKN, recessive and early onset).

blocks.title: From nigral cell loss to bradykinesia
steps: Substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons die
Striatal dopamine falls
Direct (D1) pathway weakens; indirect (D2) pathway strengthens
Globus pallidus internus inhibits the thalamus more
Thalamocortical drive to motor cortex falls
Movements become slow, small, and hard to start
blocks.caption: Both pathway changes push in the same direction, toward greater thalamic inhibition and less movement.

blocks.title: Cardinal motor signs of Parkinson disease
rows: About 4 to 6 Hz pill-rolling tremor, usually asymmetric at onset, that lessens with voluntary movement
Increased tone through the full range of passive movement (lead pipe); cogwheel when tremor is superimposed
Slow, small movements: masked face, reduced blinking, micrographia, soft voice, shuffling gait with reduced arm swing
Loss of postural reflexes, usually later in the disease, causing falls
blocks.caption: Bradykinesia plus either resting tremor or rigidity is required to call a syndrome parkinsonism.

blocks.text: Secondary parkinsonism

MPTP, a contaminant of an illicitly synthesized opioid in the early 1980s, produced sudden parkinsonism in young users. It crosses the blood-brain barrier, is oxidized by monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) in astrocytes to MPP+, and is taken up selectively into nigral neurons by the dopamine transporter. MPP+ inhibits complex I of the electron transport chain, causing ATP failure and free radical injury, a finding that supports the mitochondrial theory of PD. Drug-induced parkinsonism follows D2 receptor blockade (antipsychotics such as haloperidol, and antiemetics such as metoclopramide) or presynaptic dopamine depletion through VMAT inhibition (reserpine, tetrabenazine). Because the nigral neurons are intact, drug-induced parkinsonism tends to be symmetric, lacks Lewy bodies, and usually resolves weeks to months after the drug is stopped.

Huntington disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant disease caused by expansion of a CAG repeat in the HTT gene on the short arm of chromosome 4. CAG encodes glutamine, so the mutant huntingtin protein carries a long polyglutamine tract. It misfolds and forms nuclear inclusions, disrupts transcription and mitochondrial function, and makes striatal neurons vulnerable to glutamate excitotoxicity through NMDA receptors. This is a toxic gain of function, which is why a single mutant allele causes disease.

blocks.title: HTT CAG repeat length
rows: Intermediate: no disease in the carrier, but may expand into the disease range in offspring, mainly through the father
Full penetrance; longer repeats bring earlier onset
blocks.caption: Repeat length correlates inversely with age of onset; juvenile HD usually has more than about 60 repeats.

blocks.text: The CAG repeat is unstable during spermatogenesis, which involves many more cell divisions than oogenesis, so it tends to lengthen when passed from a father. The child then develops disease earlier and more severely than the parent, which is anticipation. Juvenile HD, often inherited paternally, presents with rigidity and bradykinesia rather than chorea.

The neurons lost first are the GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the striatum, the caudate more than the putamen. Caudate atrophy flattens the normally convex lateral walls of the frontal horns, so they look enlarged and box-shaped on imaging. Striatal GABA and acetylcholine fall, while dopamine is relatively preserved, so dopaminergic signaling is relatively excessive. The cortex is affected later.

Symptoms usually begin between about 30 and 50 years of age. Chorea consists of brief, irregular, flowing involuntary movements that move from one body part to another, with motor impersistence, such as an inability to keep the tongue protruded or maintain a steady grip. Cognitive decline is a subcortical dementia with slowed thinking and executive failure. Depression, irritability, apathy, and psychosis are common, and the suicide rate is high. Death usually follows about 15 to 20 years after onset.

blocks.title: Worked example: why Parkinson disease is slow and Huntington disease is excessive
blocks.text: Both diseases act on the same circuit. The globus pallidus internus (GPi) tonically inhibits the thalamus, and the thalamus drives the motor cortex. The direct pathway inhibits GPi, which releases the thalamus. The indirect pathway, through the external pallidum and subthalamic nucleus, excites GPi, which restrains the thalamus. In Parkinson disease, loss of dopamine weakens the direct pathway and disinhibits the indirect pathway, so GPi output rises, the thalamus is suppressed, and movement is reduced. In early Huntington disease, the striatal neurons of the indirect pathway die first. The external pallidum is released and suppresses the subthalamic nucleus, so GPi output falls, the thalamus is released, and unwanted movements (chorea) appear. Later, as direct pathway neurons also die, rigidity and bradykinesia emerge.

Friedreich ataxia is the most common inherited ataxia. It is autosomal recessive, and most patients carry an expanded GAA repeat in the first intron of FXN on chromosome 9 on both alleles. Because the repeat lies in an intron, it does not alter the protein sequence. Instead, the long GAA tract forms abnormal DNA structures and silences the gene, so too little normal frataxin is made. This is loss of function, the opposite of the toxic gain of function in Huntington disease, and it explains the recessive inheritance.

Frataxin is a mitochondrial protein needed to assemble iron-sulfur clusters, which are cofactors for aconitase and for complexes I, II, and III of the electron transport chain. Without it, iron accumulates inside mitochondria, iron-sulfur enzymes fail, ATP production falls, and free iron generates hydroxyl radicals through the Fenton reaction. The cells hurt most are large, metabolically active, nondividing cells: large dorsal root ganglion neurons, cardiomyocytes, and pancreatic beta cells.

blocks.title: From GAA expansion to cell injury
steps: GAA repeats expand in intron 1 of both FXN alleles
Transcription of FXN is silenced
Frataxin is deficient in mitochondria
Iron-sulfur cluster enzymes fail; mitochondrial iron accumulates
ATP falls and oxidative damage rises
Dorsal root ganglion neurons, cardiomyocytes, and beta cells degenerate
blocks.caption: Loss of frataxin injures tissues with high oxidative demand and little capacity to regenerate.

blocks.title: Structures damaged in Friedreich ataxia and the resulting findings
rows: Dorsal root ganglion neurons and dorsal columns
Loss of vibration and joint position sense, positive Romberg sign, sensory ataxia
Areflexia, because the afferent limb of the stretch reflex is lost
Gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus
Leg weakness and extensor plantar responses (Babinski sign)
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia, the most common cause of death
Kyphoscoliosis and pes cavus (high arch) with hammer toes, from muscle imbalance during growth
blocks.caption: Absent ankle reflexes with a Babinski sign is a characteristic combination: afferent loss abolishes the reflex while corticospinal loss produces the extensor plantar response.

blocks.text: Onset is usually in late childhood or adolescence, typically before age 25, with progressive gait ataxia as the first sign. Longer repeats, particularly on the shorter of the two alleles, bring earlier onset and more frequent cardiomyopathy. Most patients need a wheelchair within about 10 to 15 years of onset. Cognition is generally preserved.

Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, meaning it injures spinal nerve roots and peripheral nerves together. Its most common form in North America and Europe is acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP). About two thirds of patients report an infection 1 to 4 weeks earlier. Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis is the most commonly identified trigger; others include cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza, and Zika virus, and vaccination is a rare trigger.

The mechanism is molecular mimicry. Campylobacter lipooligosaccharide resembles gangliosides such as GM1 and GD1a on peripheral nerve, so antibodies raised against the bacterium bind the nerve. Complement activation and macrophages then strip myelin from Schwann cells, mainly in AIDP, or attack the axolemma at the nodes of Ranvier in the axonal variants (acute motor axonal neuropathy, linked to anti-GM1 antibodies after Campylobacter infection). Nerve roots are especially vulnerable because their blood-nerve barrier is weaker. Schwann cells can remyelinate, so most patients recover over weeks to months.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of Guillain-Barré syndrome
steps: Infection, often Campylobacter jejuni, 1 to 4 weeks earlier
Microbial antigens resemble nerve gangliosides
Antibodies, complement, and macrophages attack roots and nerves
Myelin is stripped; conduction slows or blocks
Ascending symmetric flaccid weakness with areflexia
Phrenic and autonomic fibers involved in severe cases
blocks.caption: The same immune attack explains the weakness, the lost reflexes, and the life-threatening complications.

blocks.text: Weakness is symmetric, usually begins in the legs, and ascends over days, reaching its worst point within 4 weeks. It is flaccid with reduced or absent reflexes, because conduction fails in both the afferent and efferent limbs of the stretch reflex. Distal tingling and back pain are common, but objective sensory loss is mild, with no sensory level and no early sphincter loss. Bilateral facial weakness is frequent. The Miller Fisher variant, associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies, presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia.

blocks.title: Complications and diagnostic findings
rows: Demyelination of phrenic (C3 to C5) and intercostal nerves weakens the diaphragm and chest wall; a substantial minority of patients need ventilation
Involvement of autonomic fibers causes tachycardia or bradycardia, labile blood pressure, ileus, and urinary retention
Inflamed roots leak protein into CSF, but few cells enter; protein may still be normal in the first week
Slowed conduction velocity, prolonged distal latencies, conduction block, and delayed or absent F waves (proximal root involvement)
blocks.caption: Autonomic instability and respiratory failure are the main causes of death in GBS.

blocks.predict: A patient with weakness of both legs has a sharp sensory level at the umbilicus and urinary retention. Is this Guillain-Barré syndrome?
blocks.explain: Unlikely. A sensory level and early sphincter dysfunction localize to the spinal cord, whereas GBS damages roots and nerves, causing symmetric weakness and areflexia with little objective sensory loss and no level.
blocks.check: Compare with the clinical paragraph here and with transverse myelitis (NE-20-B.12).

sections.title: Multiple sclerosis: risk, course, and findings

blocks.text: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic immune-mediated disease of the central nervous system (CNS) in which plaques of demyelination appear in different places at different times, described as dissemination in space and time. Autoreactive CD4 T cells of the Th1 and Th17 types cross the blood-brain barrier, recognize myelin antigens, and recruit macrophages and microglia, while B cells and antibodies contribute. Oligodendrocytes, which make CNS myelin, are injured, and axons are transected within plaques. Axonal loss, not demyelination alone, accounts for permanent disability.

blocks.title: Risk factors for multiple sclerosis
rows: Women are affected about two to three times as often as men
Prevalence rises with distance from the equator, linked to lower sunlight exposure and vitamin D
Prior infection is strongly associated with MS
blocks.caption: MS is thought to arise when genetically susceptible people meet environmental triggers.

blocks.text: About 85% of patients begin with a relapsing-remitting course. A relapse develops over days and resolves partly or fully over weeks as inflammation subsides, sodium channels redistribute along the demyelinated axon, and some remyelination occurs. Many later enter a secondary progressive phase, and about 10 to 15% have a primary progressive course from the start.

Myelin allows saltatory conduction because sodium channels are concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier. When myelin is lost, current leaks across the bare internode, so conduction slows or fails. Raised body temperature shortens the action potential and reduces the current available to cross the lesion, so symptoms worsen with exercise, fever, or a hot bath (Uhthoff phenomenon). Bending the neck stretches demyelinated cervical dorsal columns and produces an electric sensation down the spine or limbs (Lhermitte sign).

blocks.title: Findings in multiple sclerosis
rows: Optic nerve: painful monocular vision loss, central scotoma, reduced color vision, relative afferent pupillary defect
Medial longitudinal fasciculus; bilateral INO in a young adult strongly suggests MS
Charcot triad: nystagmus, intention tremor, scanning speech
Spinal pathways to the bladder; detrusor overactivity
Uhthoff phenomenon, from conduction block in demyelinated axons
blocks.caption: Symptoms map to white matter tracts, not to vascular territories.

blocks.text: MRI shows ovoid T2 and FLAIR hyperintense plaques in periventricular white matter, often oriented perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson fingers), and in juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord regions. Gadolinium enhancement marks active blood-brain barrier breakdown, so enhancing and nonenhancing lesions on one scan show dissemination in time. CSF shows oligoclonal IgG bands absent from serum and a raised IgG index, evidence of antibody synthesis within the CNS.

blocks.title: Worked example: localizing internuclear ophthalmoplegia
blocks.text: A 28-year-old woman looks to the right. Her right eye abducts with nystagmus, but her left eye fails to adduct. Convergence is normal. For rightward gaze, the right abducens nucleus fires the right lateral rectus and, through interneurons whose axons cross and ascend in the left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), the left oculomotor nucleus to fire the left medial rectus. Adduction works during convergence, so the left oculomotor nucleus and nerve are intact. The lesion is therefore in the left MLF, named for the side of the eye that cannot adduct: a left INO. In a young adult, especially if bilateral, the classic cause is an MS plaque; in an older adult, a brainstem infarct is more likely.

sections.title: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis versus multiple sclerosis

blocks.text: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is an acute, usually single episode of immune-mediated inflammatory demyelination of the brain and spinal cord. It occurs mostly in children and typically follows a viral infection by days to a few weeks; measles, varicella, rubella, mumps, influenza, and nonspecific upper respiratory infections are classic antecedents. Vaccination is a rare trigger. Older rabies vaccines grown in animal nervous tissue caused it by injecting myelin antigens, the same principle used to induce experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis in animals.

Molecular mimicry or nonspecific activation of the immune system generates T cells that react against myelin, and the attack occurs once. Microscopically, sleeves of lymphocytes and macrophages surround small veins, with demyelination confined to these perivenular zones, and all lesions are the same age. MS, by contrast, forms confluent plaques with sharp borders, and lesions of different ages coexist. Acute hemorrhagic leukoencephalitis is a rare, hyperacute and often fatal form with necrotizing vasculitis of venules and hemorrhage.

Clinically, ADEM produces sudden multifocal deficits together with encephalopathy (confusion, drowsiness, or behavioral change), often with fever, headache, and seizures. Encephalopathy is required for the diagnosis and is unusual in an MS relapse. A subset of children have antibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG). New demyelinating events more than about 3 months later prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis, including MS.

blocks.title: ADEM compared with multiple sclerosis
rows: None identifiable; genetic and environmental risk
Perivenular demyelination, lesions all the same age
Confluent sharply bordered plaques of different ages
Large, poorly marginated, bilateral lesions, often involving the thalami and basal ganglia; all enhance alike if they enhance
Ovoid periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, and cord lesions; mixed enhancing and nonenhancing lesions
Lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein; oligoclonal bands usually absent or transient
Persistent oligoclonal bands and raised IgG index
blocks.caption: One attack after an infection in a child favors ADEM; repeated attacks over years in a young adult favor MS.

sections.title: Dementia with Lewy bodies, frontotemporal dementia, and progressive supranuclear palsy

blocks.text: Each neurodegenerative dementia is defined by the protein that aggregates and the region where it collects. Alpha-synuclein diseases are synucleinopathies, tau diseases are tauopathies, and a third group accumulates TDP-43. The region involved first decides the earliest symptoms.
Dementia with Lewy bodies

In dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies form in limbic and neocortical neurons as well as in the brainstem. Cortical Lewy bodies are less distinct than nigral ones and lack the halo, and coexisting AD pathology is common. Core features are fluctuating cognition with marked swings in attention and alertness, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism. Attention, executive, and visuospatial deficits appear early, while memory is relatively spared at first. Patients are highly sensitive to D2-blocking drugs, which can sharply worsen rigidity and confusion. By convention, dementia that begins before or within 1 year of parkinsonism is DLB, while dementia that appears more than a year after established PD is Parkinson disease dementia.
Frontotemporal dementia

Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) results from frontotemporal lobar degeneration, with atrophy of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes that can thin gyri to a knife edge. Onset is often between 45 and 65, younger than typical AD. The behavioral variant causes early disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behavior, and hyperorality; language variants cause progressive aphasia. Memory and visuospatial skills are relatively preserved early, the reverse of AD. Pathology is either tau, including Pick disease with round silver-staining Pick bodies and swollen Pick cells, or TDP-43 inclusions, the group that includes C9orf72 cases and links FTD with ALS.
Progressive supranuclear palsy

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a tauopathy with neurofibrillary tangles and tufted astrocytes in the subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, midbrain tectum, and dentate nucleus. Midbrain atrophy produces the hummingbird sign on sagittal MRI. Damage to midbrain vertical gaze centers causes vertical gaze palsy, downgaze first; it is supranuclear because the oculocephalic reflex still moves the eyes. Axial rigidity with neck extension and early unexplained backward falls, usually within the first year, are typical, with dysarthria, dysphagia, and frontal executive decline. Tremor is uncommon, and response to dopamine replacement is poor because striatal and pallidal neurons are also lost.

blocks.title: Dementias defined by protein and region
rows: Personality and behavior change or aphasia
Vertical gaze palsy and early backward falls
blocks.caption: Lewy bodies are alpha-synuclein; Pick bodies are tau.

sections.title: Vascular dementia and mild cognitive impairment

blocks.text: Vascular dementia is cognitive decline caused by cerebrovascular disease and is the second most common dementia after AD. In multi-infarct dementia, repeated cortical or subcortical infarcts each remove a block of tissue, so the course is stepwise: an abrupt drop after each stroke, then a plateau or partial recovery. A single infarct in a strategic site, such as the thalamus, can also cause dementia. Diffuse small vessel disease from hypertensive arteriolosclerosis causes lacunes and widespread ischemic white matter injury, the subcortical form also called Binswanger disease, and can produce a more gradual decline. Risk factors are those of stroke: hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, and atrial fibrillation.

Vascular injury mainly disconnects frontal-subcortical circuits, so slowed processing, poor attention, and executive dysfunction dominate, and memory retrieval is impaired more than storage. In AD, hippocampal damage prevents encoding, so cues and recognition do not rescue recall. Vascular dementia is accompanied by focal signs such as hemiparesis, a Babinski sign, a short-stepped gait, pseudobulbar affect, and urinary urgency, and imaging shows infarcts and white matter hyperintensities. Many older adults have both AD and vascular pathology (mixed dementia).

Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is a decline in one or more cognitive domains greater than expected for age and education, reported by the person or an informant and confirmed by testing, with independence in daily activities preserved. Complex tasks may take longer, but the person still manages them. That preserved function is what separates MCI from dementia. MCI is a risk state rather than a disease: the amnestic type in particular often progresses to AD, at about 10 to 15% per year in clinic populations, while some people remain stable or improve. Reversible contributors such as depression, hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, sedating medications, and sleep apnea must be considered.

blocks.title: Normal aging, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia compared
rows: Below expected for age and education
Impaired in memory and other domains
Impaired, especially executive and processing speed
Gradual; may progress, remain stable, or revert
Often abrupt and stepwise; gradual with small vessel disease
Encoding failure; cues do not help
blocks.caption: Function decides dementia versus MCI; time course and focal signs separate vascular from Alzheimer dementia.

blocks.text: Transverse myelitis is acute or subacute inflammation across both halves of one or a few segments of the spinal cord, most often in the thoracic cord. Deficits develop over hours to days and peak within about 3 weeks. Many cases are postinfectious or idiopathic, following viral infections (herpes simplex, varicella zoster, Epstein-Barr, cytomegalovirus, enteroviruses) or Mycoplasma. Others occur with MS, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (aquaporin-4 antibodies), MOG antibody disease, or systemic autoimmune disease such as systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren syndrome, and sarcoidosis. Lymphocytes and macrophages infiltrate the cord, damaging myelin, axons, and gray matter.
Because the lesion crosses the cord, every long tract passing through that level is interrupted on both sides, which explains the three signature findings.

blocks.title: Cord structures injured and resulting findings
rows: Bilateral weakness (paraparesis with thoracic lesions, quadriparesis with cervical lesions); flaccid with absent reflexes during spinal shock (motor neurons below the lesion are briefly unexcitable), later spastic with hyperreflexia and Babinski signs
Sensory level: reduced pain, temperature, vibration, and position sense below a dermatome, often with a band of altered sensation at the level
Descending autonomic pathways to sacral and thoracolumbar centers
Bladder dysfunction: early urinary retention, later urgency and incontinence from detrusor overactivity, plus bowel and sexual dysfunction
Back pain at the level of the lesion
blocks.caption: Bilateral weakness, a sensory level, and bladder dysfunction together localize to the spinal cord.

blocks.text: Compression of the cord by an epidural abscess, tumor, hematoma, or disc produces the same picture and must be excluded with MRI. In transverse myelitis, MRI shows T2 hyperintensity within the cord, often enhancing, and CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein, sometimes with a raised IgG index. Lesion length helps identify the cause: MS typically produces partial, asymmetric lesions shorter than two vertebral segments in the peripheral cord, whereas neuromyelitis optica produces complete, central lesions spanning three or more segments (longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis). The sensory level distinguishes transverse myelitis from GBS, which has no level, and an anterior spinal artery infarct differs by its sudden onset and sparing of the dorsal columns.

blocks.predict: Why are reflexes absent in the legs in the first days after severe transverse myelitis, even though the corticospinal tracts are cut?
blocks.explain: Spinal shock: abrupt loss of descending input leaves spinal motor neurons and interneurons below the lesion transiently unexcitable. As they recover over days to weeks, UMN signs of spasticity and hyperreflexia appear.

sections.title: Essential tremor, other tremors, and cervical dystonia

blocks.text: A tremor is an involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of a body part produced by alternating or synchronous contraction of opposing muscles. Tremors are classified by when they occur: at rest, while holding a posture against gravity, or during movement (kinetic tremor, which includes intention tremor that worsens near a target). The condition under which a tremor appears points to the circuit at fault.

Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder. It is often familial with an autosomal dominant pattern. It causes a bilateral, fairly symmetric postural and action tremor of the hands and forearms, often with head tremor (yes-yes or no-no) and voice tremor. It worsens with stress, fatigue, and caffeine, and in many patients it improves briefly after a small amount of alcohol. Other neurologic signs are classically absent. Handwriting is large and shaky, in contrast to the small handwriting (micrographia) of Parkinson disease. The tremor is thought to arise from abnormal oscillation in the cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit.

blocks.title: Tremors compared
rows: At rest; lessens with voluntary movement
Holding a posture and during action
During goal-directed movement; worse near the target
Asymmetric hand, pill-rolling; may involve jaw or legs, rarely head
Bilateral hands; head and voice often
Limb on the same side as the cerebellar lesion
Loss of substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons
Ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere, dentate nucleus, or superior cerebellar peduncle (MS, stroke, alcohol)
blocks.caption: Ask when the tremor appears: at rest, while holding a posture, or while reaching a target.

blocks.text: Dystonia is sustained or intermittent involuntary muscle contraction that produces twisting movements and abnormal postures. Cervical dystonia is the most common focal dystonia in adults, usually beginning between about 30 and 50 years and more often in women. Rotation of the head is torticollis; tilt, flexion, and extension are laterocollis, anterocollis, and retrocollis. Contraction of one sternocleidomastoid turns the face toward the opposite side, usually with the contralateral splenius capitis. Neck pain and a jerky head tremor are common, and a light touch to the chin or face (a sensory trick) can briefly reduce the contraction. Imaging is usually normal; the disorder reflects abnormal basal ganglia output, reduced inhibition in motor circuits, and faulty sensorimotor integration. It differs from congenital muscular torticollis, fibrosis of one sternocleidomastoid in an infant, and from acute dystonic reactions caused by D2-blocking drugs.

integration.text: Across this chapter, the same few principles recur. Neurodegenerative diseases are protein-folding diseases: amyloid beta and tau in AD, alpha-synuclein in PD and DLB, tau in PSP and some FTD, TDP-43 in most ALS and the rest of FTD, and polyglutamine huntingtin in HD. Biochemistry explains the selectivity: nigral neurons handle oxidizable dopamine, frataxin-deficient cells fail because their mitochondria cannot build iron-sulfur clusters, and long neurons depend on intact microtubule transport. Genetics explains the inheritance: toxic gain of function (HTT, SOD1, APP) acts dominantly, while loss of function (FXN) is recessive, and unstable repeats explain anticipation in HD. Anatomy then turns each lesion into signs, from the basal ganglia pathways to the MLF and the long tracts of the cord.

Immunology unifies the demyelinating diseases, but the target cell sets the pattern. Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons, so MS, ADEM, and transverse myelitis cause tract signs, sensory levels, and UMN findings, while Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves, so GBS causes flaccid areflexic weakness. Molecular mimicry links infection to GBS and ADEM, and intrathecal antibody synthesis gives MS its oligoclonal bands. Limits matter: overlap pathology is common in older brains, clinical diagnosis during life is probabilistic, and certainty about protein type often comes only at autopsy.

summary: In AD, beta then gamma secretase (presenilin) cleave APP into amyloid beta 42, which forms plaques; hyperphosphorylated tau forms tangles that correlate with dementia.
AD risk rises with age, APOE e4, trisomy 21 (extra APP), and dominant APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2 mutations; hippocampal involvement makes short-term memory loss the first symptom.
AD atrophy enlarges the ventricles passively (hydrocephalus ex vacuo), and amyloid angiopathy causes lobar hemorrhage in older adults.
ALS combines UMN and LMN signs in the same region with sensation, sphincters, and eye movements spared, and ends in respiratory failure.
PD is loss of nigral dopaminergic neurons with alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies, increasing thalamic inhibition; MPTP (via MPP+ and complex I) and D2 blockade cause secondary parkinsonism.
HD is an autosomal dominant CAG expansion in HTT on chromosome 4 that destroys caudate GABAergic neurons, causing chorea, dementia, and depression, with paternal anticipation.

Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive intronic GAA expansion in FXN causing frataxin loss and mitochondrial iron overload, with ataxia, areflexia plus Babinski signs, and fatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
GBS is post-infectious molecular mimicry against peripheral myelin, causing ascending flaccid areflexic weakness and high CSF protein with normal cells; respiratory and autonomic failure kill.

MS affects women aged 20 to 40 at higher latitudes with relapsing plaques of different ages: optic neuritis, INO, heat-worsened symptoms, periventricular MRI lesions, and oligoclonal bands; ADEM is a single perivenular attack in a child after infection.

Lewy bodies with hallucinations and fluctuations mean DLB, early personality change means FTD, vertical gaze palsy with falls means PSP, stepwise decline means vascular dementia, and preserved function means MCI; tremor at rest, with posture, or near a target points to PD, essential tremor, or cerebellar disease.

verify: Proportion of Alzheimer disease that is autosomal dominant is quoted from under 1% to about 5% in different sources; this chapter says only a small minority.

HTT repeat thresholds (26 or fewer normal, 27 to 35 intermediate, 36 to 39 reduced penetrance, 40 or more full penetrance) follow common genetic consensus; review books sometimes give a single cutoff near 36 to 40.

The degree of nigral neuron and striatal dopamine loss before motor signs appear is quoted from about 50% to 80% in different sources; stated here as roughly half of nigral neurons and most striatal dopamine.
Female to male ratio in MS is quoted from about 2:1 to 3:1; relapsing-remitting onset about 85% and primary progressive about 10 to 15% are approximate.
Annual progression of MCI to dementia (about 10 to 15% per year in clinic samples) varies widely with the population studied.
The time to nadir in transverse myelitis (about 3 weeks, from consensus diagnostic criteria) and the interval for ADEM after infection vary between sources.
Essential tremor frequency range (about 4 to 12 Hz) and cerebellar tremor frequency (usually below 5 Hz) are approximate and differ slightly between texts.
